description:
Somos un equipo apasionado por la tecnología, la inteligencia artificial, el espacio y la agricultura sostenible.

Para la NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 nos hemos propuesto trabajar en el desafío Field Shift, explorando cómo podemos utilizar los datos satelitales de la NASA y la inteligencia artificial para ayudar a los agricultores a tomar mejores decisiones sobre sus cultivos, el suelo y el clima.

¡Estamos buscando personas con ganas de aportar ideas, aprender y, sobre todo, pasarlo bien!
summary:
ORCHID, short for Orbital Rotation & Crop Health Intelligent Decision Platform is a web application built to help U.S. Farmers make crop rotation choices that boost soil health and climate resilience. ORCHID was created for the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data competition. ORCHID shows how data from Earth observation can be turned into farm decisions by blending NASA satellite images, USDA soil and agriculture data and details that belong to each farm.

ORCHID currently works in the United States, where many agricultural and environmental datasets can be easily accessed. ORCHID first shows its power, in Kansas and Iowa two farming states where ORCHID sees a lot of chances to make a difference.

Farmers can choose their fields on a satellite map. Then get at least three crop rotation plans, one of which is the farmer’s current practice. ORCHID gives each plan an explanation of the evidence, possible benefits, possible risks and missing data all scored by a simple rule‑based engine that is easy to understand.

ORCHID turns environmental data into clear actions. ORCHID lets farmers try varied crop rotations manage water better protect soil health and adjust to a changing climate.

ORCHID hopes to grow beyond the United States. ORCHID plans to bring the platform to countries by adding more local and global data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ORCHID is a web‑based decision‑support platform that helps U.S. Farmers plan crop rotations to improve soil health optimize water use and build resilience to changing climate.

Farmers begin by searching a town or ZIP code and picking a field on a satellite map. Farmers then give details like field size, irrigation availability and crops grown in the last one or two years. Farmers may also input yields, crop prices and production costs so that ORCHID can calculate farm‑specific economic estimates.

ORCHID then:

  • Compares crop rotation scenarios: ORCHID evaluates at least three alternatives, including the farmers current practices as a baseline. ORCHID classifies recommendations as "Best Option," " as Good " or "Riskier."
  • Explains every recommendation: ORCHID provides the reasoning for each scenario the supporting evidence, potential benefits, associated risks and missing information that farmers or local agricultural experts should examine.
  • Ensures transparency and traceability: ORCHID clearly separates original source data from calculations. ORCHID links each data point back to its source and the downloadable report records the scoring criteria, rules and weights that ORCHID uses.
  • Provides estimates: ORCHID calculates potential profit or loss per acre using the farmers own economic inputs. If state‑level USDA crop prices are available ORCHID can use them too. ORCHID never invents figures. ORCHID estimates are scenarios, not guaranteed outcomes and their accuracy depends on how complete and reliable the inputs are.
  • Generates field‑specific reports: ORCHID lets farmers download and print reports that include recommendations, supporting evidence, calculations and limitations.
  • Includes Brote, an assistant: Brote answers questions in text or voice in English and Spanish. Brote uses the data sources and tools that ORCHID uses cites the sources for any numbers it gives and clearly says when information is missing.

HOW IT WORKS

When a farmer selects a field ORCHID’s backend pulls and processes data from NASA and agricultural sources at the same time. These datasets give information about climate, vegetation, soil, water, topography and local farming practices.

NASA Earth Observation and Environmental Data

  • NASA POWER (2015–2024): monthly precipitation, temperature and root‑zone soil moisture indicators. ORCHID combines these variables into a normalized 0–1 monthly climate‑stress index that captures periods of heat, low rainfall and soil moisture stress.
  • MODIS NDVI (MOD13Q1 250 m every 16 days): This data tracks vegetation activity. Points out times when bare soil might appear during the year.
  • SMAP L3 (9 km): This provides satellite‑based surface soil moisture measurements.
  • GPM IMERG Late (0.1°): This gives satellite‑derived precipitation estimates for the 30 days.
  • NLDAS‑2 Noah: This supplies soil moisture estimates down to about 1 meter enabling comparison of conditions with a 10‑year historical baseline.
  • SRTM (30 m): This gives elevation and slope data that ORCHID uses to evaluate erosion risk.

Agricultural Data Sources

  • - USDA SSURGO: This gives soil texture, drainage characteristics and water‑holding capacity.
  • - USDA Cropland Data Layer (2021–2025): This shows crop distribution and past farming patterns.
  • - GAEZ v4: This offers crop suitability and growing‑season information drawn from data.
  • - CoCoRaHS: This uses observations from volunteer rain gauges letting local precipitation measurements be compared with NASA POWER estimates.

Data Integration and Spatial Limitations

The integrated datasets differ in resolution, time coverage and measurement style. For example MODIS gives vegetation data at 250 m resolution while SMAP gives soil moisture at about 9 km resolution. Thus not every dataset shows a measurement for each field.

ORCHID blends field‑level data, with regional and environmental indicators keeping these differences in mind when it interprets results. ORCHID tells users that data availability and resolution vary by location so users do not overestimate how precise the information is.

Crop Rotation Recommendation Engine

I see the ORCHID system as a rule‑based scoring engine that evaluates eight crop options: corn, soybeans, winter wheat, sorghum, sunflower, oats, cereal rye and clover as a cover crop.

The engine considers factors:

  • I note historical crop rotation patterns, such as crop families and legume-after-grass sequences.
  • I consider water stress during the crop growing cycle.
  • I look at soil texture. How much water it can hold.
  • I check times when bare soil might be exposed.
  • I assess terrain slope and risk of erosion.
  • I notice soil moisture levels.
  • I observe patterns of crop adoption in the area.
  • I use inputs provided by the farmer.

I see the system looking at crop and cover‑crop combinations to create rotation scenarios. Every recommendation shows its scores and the reasoning behind it.

I find that the scoring rules, weights and assumptions are shown in the report. The recommendation engine is still experimental. Has not been formally validated by agronomists. Its purpose is to give evidence‑based decision help not to replace professional agronomic advice. Getting validation from agricultural extension specialists is a next step.

BENEFITS

  • Turns data into practical insights: I see it as bringing together satellite, climate and soil data to give clear agricultural recommendations.
  • Supports informed decision‑making: I see it as offering many alternatives instead of one fixed answer letting farmers compare trade‑offs.
  • Promotes transparency: I notice it shows data sources, calculations, assumptions, uncertainties and potential risks.
  • Connects environmental and economic factors: I see it helping farmers look at sustainable crop rotations while thinking about their own costs, yields and possible profits.
  • Improves accessibility: I see it working in English and Spanish letting farmers use voice or text and using U.S. Units like acres, bushels and dollars per acre.
  • Provides an easy experience: I see it running in a web browser with light and dark modes and the demo can be tried without an account.

Geographic Scope

I understand that the ORCHID system focuses on the United States, where many agricultural and environmental datasetsre available. Kansas and Iowa are the regions we show, chosen for their farming relevance and potential impact.

Even though the platform aims for U.S. Coverage, data and map detail differ by region. Our long‑term goal is to reach countries by adding more regional and international data.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

I think the ORCHID goal is to encourage diverse crop rotations and more cover‑crop use especially on farms that leave soil bare for long times or keep planting the same crops.

By helping farmers see the economic trade‑offs of different rotations I hope to reduce soil erosion improve water flow manage soil moisture better and build more resilience to drought and climate change.

Our next steps include:

  • Validation: I work with agronomists and extension teams especially at Iowa State University and Kansas State University to validate and improve the recommendation rules.
  • Expanding coverage: I add more crops, rotation strategies, regions, countries and among others.
  • Improving observation: I add data, such as ESA Sentinel‑2 to better monitor vegetation and map detail.
  • International expansion: I bring in more regional and international data so ORCHID can reach farmers in other countries.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Frontend

  • Next.js 16 React and TypeScript.
  • Tailwind CSS v4.
  • MapLibre GL for geospatial visualization.
  • Recharts for data visualization.
  • Web Speech API for voice interactions.

Backend

  • Python and FastAPI.
  • Postgresql.
  • NumPy for processing.

NASA Data Integration

  • NASA Earthdata Login and Common Metadata Repository (CMR).
  • Cloud OPeNDAP (Hyrax).
  • ORNL DAAC MODIS subset API.
  • NASA POWER API.

Cloud. Ai

  • Azure Container Apps.
  • Azure Database for PostgreSQL.
  • Azure AI Foundry (gpt-5-mini) powering Brote.

GitHub Actions, for CI/CD using Connect (OIDC) authentication.

HOW TO TRY IT

  1. Open the ORCHID web application.
  2. Click "Try the demo without an account."
  3. Search, for "Ames, Iowa."
  4. Choose a field on the satellite map.
  5. Enter the field size in acres.
  6. Click "See what I should plant."
  7. Explore the recommended crop rotation scenarios. Download the field report.

Brote, the AI assistant needs an account.

Links

  • Live application: https://orchid-web.lemonwater-87aebdb5.eastus2.azurecontainerapps.io/
  • Source code: https://github.com/CamiloAndresDG/orchid_app
  • Team: Orbital Farmers.

Project Name

ORCHID stands for Orbital Rotation & Crop Health Intelligent Decision Platform. The name also honors Colombias flower, the orchid (Cattleya trianae) showing the Colombian roots of the team.

ALERT

It may take a while to open the first time, as it is currently suspended to avoid excessive Azure credit consumption. It finishes loading in about 10 seconds, and after that, it remains open.
